issues.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land is assessed from reliable transactions near the acquisition date, with adjustments for timing and the size of the acquired parcel.
material_facts: The acquired land was part of a larger holding, and the owner had purchased land in the same survey number and later sold one acre of it in a genuine transaction at a price substantially below the compensation claimed.
The acquisition covered more than five acres and followed the sale by about nine months.
The lower courts relied on an award for different land acquired earlier and disregarded the sale transactions concerning the acquired land.
issues.conclusion: The market value at the notification date was fixed by taking the genuine sale of land in the same holding as the principal evidence and allowing for the time gap; the larger acquired block would not command a higher rate than the smaller parcel sold.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is the price a willing vendor could reasonably expect from a willing purchaser on the date of publication of the Section 4(1) notification. A sale or purchase of the acquired land within a reasonable time is the best evidence; absent that, transactions involving land with similar advantages in the neighbourhood may be used. The Court relied on Periya & Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala, [1990] Supp. 1 SCR 362.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and genuine_nearby_sale_of_acquired_land and sale_close_in_time_to_notification and acquired_parcel_larger_than_sold_parcel

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.genuine_nearby_sale_of_acquired_land: A genuine sale of the acquired land or land in the same holding took place.
predicates.sale_close_in_time_to_notification: The sale occurred sufficiently near the acquisition notification to provide evidence of value at that time.
predicates.acquired_parcel_larger_than_sold_parcel: The area acquired as a block was larger than the parcel sold in the relied-on transaction.

issues.definition: When a compensation case has a genuine, timely sale of the acquired land and the acquired block is larger than the sold parcel, the market value is based on that sale with appropriate adjustments.

issues.legal_issue: A deduction for development is appropriate when acquired land for a housing layout requires land to be set aside for roads and other amenities.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a housing scheme and covered a substantial area.
The Court considered the need to provide roads, drainage, electricity and other amenities in developing land for building colonies.
The Court held that one-third of the assessed market value should be deducted for development in this case.
issues.conclusion: One-third of the market value was deducted for development, reducing the compensation valuation accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: A development deduction depends on the situation of the land and the need for development; it is not justified where the acquired land is already developed with amenities. The Court relied on Tribeni Devi v. Collector of Ranchi, [1972] 3 SCR 208; Kaushalya Devi Bogre v. Land Acquisition Officer, [1984] 2 SCR 900; Vijay Kumar Motilal v. State of Maharashtra, [1981] 2 SCC 719; Vijaysingh Liladhar v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, [1983] 3 SCC 760; Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. T. Adinarayan Setty, [1959] Supp. 1 SCR 404; Special Tehsildar, Visakhapatnam v. Rednam Dharma Rao; and Tehsildar, Land Acquisition, Visakhapatnam v. P. Narasing Rao, [1985] 1 APLJ 99.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and land_acquired_for_housing_layout and development_amenities_needed and not land_already_developed_with_amenities

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.land_acquired_for_housing_layout: The acquired land is intended for a housing layout or scheme.
predicates.development_amenities_needed: Developing the land requires provision of roads, drainage, electricity or other amenities.
predicates.land_already_developed_with_amenities: The acquired land is already developed with the relevant roads and amenities.

issues.definition: When acquired land for a housing layout needs development amenities and is not already developed with them, a development deduction is applied to its market value.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may correct a lower court's land valuation when it applies a valuation principle wrongly or overlooks material factors affecting value.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the valuation fixed by the lower courts.
The lower courts disregarded genuine sale transactions concerning the acquired land and relied on an award concerning different land.
The High Court also failed to make the development deduction that the Court found appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The Court exercised its appellate power to correct the valuation and allowed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court may correct a valuation where a lower court has wrongly applied a principle or overlooked or misapplied important points affecting valuation. The Court relied on Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. T. Adinarayan Setty, [1959] Supp. 1 SCR 404; Dattatrayaya Shankarbhat Ambalgi v. Collector of Sholapur, AIR 1970 SC 850; The Dollar Co., Madras v. Collector of Madras, [1975] Supp. SCC 403; and Padma Uppal v. State of Punjab, [1977] 1 SCR 329.

predicates.land_acquisition_valuation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the valuation of land acquired by the State.
predicates.lower_court_wrongly_applied_valuation_pr: A lower court applied a principle governing land valuation incorrectly.
predicates.material_valuation_factors_overlooked: A lower court overlooked or misapplied important facts affecting the valuation.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning acquired-land valuation, if a lower court wrongly applies a valuation principle and overlooks material valuation factors, the Supreme Court corrects the valuation.
